questions.question: Which statement is the nonnegativity axiom?
questions.explanation: The nonnegativity axiom states that probabilities are never negative: $P(A)\ge0$ for every event $A$.

questions.question: Can a valid probability measure assign $P(A)=1$ to an event $A\neq S$?
questions.explanation: Yes: $P(A)=1$ only forces $P(A^c)=0$, not $A=S$. For a continuous random variable, $P(X\neq c)=1$ even though the event $\{X\neq c\}$ is not the whole sample space.

'No, never' is the same misconception; probability $1$ means 'almost certain', which does not require the event to be all of $S$.
$A=\emptyset$ has probability $0$, the opposite of $1$.

questions.question: For any two events (not necessarily disjoint), the axioms imply that $P(A\cup B)$ is:
questions.explanation: By inclusion–exclusion, $P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)$, and since $P(A\cap B)\ge0$ this gives the subadditivity bound $P(A\cup B)\le P(A)+P(B)$.

$\ge P(A)+P(B)$ is the wrong direction: a union cannot be more probable than the sum of the parts.
$P(A)P(B)$ is the product (the intersection under independence), not the union.

questions.explanation: Monotonicity: if $A\subseteq B$ then $B=A\cup(B\setminus A)$ with disjoint parts, so $P(B)=P(A)+P(B\setminus A)\ge P(A)$, i.e. $P(A)\le P(B)$.
